claims.text: Pre-coating W particles with a thin Ni interlayer before consolidation into Cu promotes better wetting at the W–Cu interface.
A Ni interlayer promotes interfacial diffusion between W and Cu.
Pre-coating W particles reduces void formation and phase separation during sintering.
The coating reduces void formation and phase separation during irradiation service.
Mechanical alloying or SPS of W–Cu typically produces interfacial voids and chemical inhomogeneity.
A uniform thin Ni coating can be applied to W particles by vapor deposition or electroless plating.
The proposed coated W–Cu powder composite can be consolidated by spark-plasma sintering.
A continuous thin interfacial layer at the W–Cu boundary enhances wettability.
A continuous thin interfacial layer enables improved atomic interdiffusion at the W–Cu boundary.
The interlayer lowers the interfacial free energy between W and Cu.
The interlayer acts as a diffusion bridge between W and Cu.
Enhanced interfacial bonding minimizes voids and phase separation during sintering and irradiation-induced thermal cycling.
The interlayer preserves the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
Relative to uncoated W in Cu, the coated composite will have fewer interfacial voids and defects.
Reduced interfacial defects will improve thermal transport.
The coated composite will maintain high mechanical durability under irradiation relative to an uncoated control.
Uncoated W–Cu composites made by mechanical alloying, SPS, or casting typically suffer phase separation and void formation.
The intervention is expected to be effective for fine, powder-based SPS consolidation in fusion heat-transfer applications.
